definition.en: Roman governor of a senatorial province (e.g. Cyprus, Achaia), serving a usually one-year term. Luke's correct use of this title for Sergius Paulus and Gallio reflects accurate provincial knowledge.
The Roman official governing the imperial province of Judea. Pilate's correct title was 'prefect' (praefectus), as the Pilate Stone shows; later governors were styled 'procurator'.
A ruler of a quarter or portion of a kingdom — the title of Herod Antipas (Galilee and Perea) and his brother Philip, sons of Herod the Great, during Jesus' ministry.
The supreme Jewish council and court in Jerusalem, led by the high priest, with authority over religious and many civil matters under Roman oversight.
A local Jewish assembly and place of Scripture reading and prayer. Paul's standard strategy was to preach first in the synagogue of each city, reaching both Jews and Gentile 'God-fearers'.
Gentiles attracted to Judaism who attended the synagogue and kept some practices without full conversion. They formed a receptive audience for Paul's message across the Diaspora.
The dispersion of Jews living outside the land of Israel throughout the Greco-Roman world. Its network of synagogues gave the early mission its ready-made routes and audiences.

The roughly two centuries of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire that, with safe roads and sea lanes and a common Greek tongue, enabled the rapid spread of the early Christian message.
The major Roman road across Macedonia linking the Adriatic to Byzantium, passing through Philippi, Amphipolis and Thessalonica — the highway Paul travelled on the second journey.

The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures used widely in the Diaspora and quoted throughout the New Testament; it made the Jewish Scriptures accessible to Greek-speaking Gentiles. Its Genesis 5 and 11 figures are longer than the Hebrew Masoretic text, so a chronology read from the Greek puts Creation and the Flood roughly a thousand years earlier than Ussher's 4004 BC / 2348 BC.
A league of ten Hellenistic cities, mostly east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. Jesus ministered in this largely Gentile region (e.g. the Gerasene demoniac, Mark 5).
The 'Hill of Ares' (Mars Hill) in Athens and the council associated with it, before which Paul delivered his address to the philosophers (Acts 17:22–31).
A civic magistrate of Macedonian cities. Luke's use of 'politarchs' for Thessalonica's rulers (Acts 17:6) was once doubted but is confirmed by numerous inscriptions.
The day of Passover in the Hebrew calendar. Dating the crucifixion depends partly on which years Nisan 14 fell near a Friday under Pilate — yielding the candidate years AD 30 and AD 33.

term.en: The age of the Earth (Genesis 5 and 11)

definition.en: Scripture never writes 'the Earth is N years old' in a single verse. It gives father-to-son intervals in Genesis 5 (Adam to Noah) and Genesis 11 (Shem to Abraham). On the Masoretic numbers those intervals are 1,656 years from Adam to the Flood; Ussher placed Creation on 23 October 4004 BC and the Flood in 2348 BC, so the Earth is about six thousand years old on this reckoning. The Septuagint's longer figures push Creation and Flood roughly a millennium earlier; the Samaritan Pentateuch differs again. Archaeology dates the human layers that follow — flood silt, early cities, Judah's waterworks — not the forming of the planet, and those layers sit in the same story rather than as a rival clock.
